relations.myth: Morotí and Pitá become the irupé
relations.note: Irupé’s Morotí incarnation loves Pitá and joins him in the flower.

relations.myth: Morotí and Pitá become the irupé
relations.note: Morotí’s transformed body forms the flower’s white inner petals.
Morotí enters the Paraná to recover Pitá from her enchantment.

relations.myth: The maiden pursues the Moon’s reflection
relations.note: The moon-lover seeks Jasy, embraces its reflection, and drowns.
Tupá pities the drowned lover and changes her or him into irupé.
Naiá occupies the corresponding Brazilian heroine role but is not identical historically.

relations.myth: Jaci makes Naiá the star of waters
relations.note: In the Brazilian cognate, Jaci transforms the drowned heroine into vitória-régia.
Panambí loves Irupé and imagines becoming a butterfly to caress her.
Akãhatã is the rival warrior opposing the lovers.
The personified river courts and embraces Irupé as its vegetable bride.

relations.myth: The river creates its vegetable bride
relations.note: The personified Paraná supplies the agency for the maiden’s floral transformation.
They are paired pedagogically as Indigenous heroines transformed into regional flowers.
Both belong to the literary genre linking Indigenous heroines with flowers.
